Chapter 3 — Building the Picture from Scratch

Causal Analysis in Public Health Management | BK Advisors

Matthew Luke Kuch | BK Advisors

2026-04-18

Meet Faith

Faith, 29, M&E officer, Turkana County, Kenya (a composite drawn from county health reports — the details are real, the name is not)

Faith has been the monitoring and evaluation officer for Turkana’s maternal health programme for two years.

Her job is to figure out what is working. Her tools are a laptop, a notebook, and a budget for petrol.

Last month her county director walked into her office and asked one sentence: “Why is our maternal mortality not falling as fast as the neighbouring county’s?”

The question: How do you build a useful causal picture for a programme you have never studied — in two weeks, with no prior research, and with people who do not speak the language of statistics?

And here is the puzzle

Kenya devolved health to 47 counties in 2013 (Constitution of Kenya, Schedule 4).

Since then, some counties have cut maternal mortality dramatically. Others have barely moved (Kenya Health Information System, county dashboards).

The county-level numbers can tell you which counties are improving. They cannot tell you why.

To find out why, you have to go talk to people. The question is — who, and in what order, and what do you do with what they tell you?

The interview method

Three rules before you walk in

  1. Start with the outcome, not the programme. Ask everyone the same opening question: “When a mother dies in this county, what is the most common chain of events?”
  2. Listen for nouns. Sketch them as boxes. Every noun a person uses — referral form, fuel, stockout, husband’s permission — is a candidate for a box.
  3. Ask the connecting question. After every box: “And what does that depend on?”

You are not running a survey. You are building a picture — and the picture is the deliverable.

Faith’s first interview — the midwife

Faith starts with Mary, a midwife at a rural facility two hours from the county town.

She asks the opening question. Mary thinks. Then she says:

mary

“Most of the deaths I see come down to this — the woman bleeds at home, the family waits four hours hoping it will stop, by the time they get a motorbike to bring her here, she has lost too much blood. We have the drugs. We do not have her in time.”

Listen for nouns: bleeding, family, waiting, motorbike, drugs, time.

Mary’s picture, in boxes


Bleeding starts at home → Family waits → Motorbike arranged → Mother arrives too late → Mother dies

This is a chain — exactly the shape you learned in Chapter 2.

The nouns become boxes. The order of events becomes the arrows. That is the whole trick.

Faith’s second interview — the husband

Next, Faith meets Lokol, whose wife survived a difficult delivery six months ago.

She asks the same opening question.

lokol

“My wife was bleeding. I knew she needed to go. But in our compound, my older brother is the elder — he is the one who decides about big expenses. And he was at the market that day. I am her husband, but I am not the elder of the compound. I had to wait until he came back to give permission to spend the money on transport. By then it was very late.”

A new noun appears: permission. It was not on Mary’s picture. But it sits before the motorbike box, and it changes the meaning of “family waits”. (In Lokol’s extended-family compound, the older brother holds financial authority — a real pattern in many rural Kenyan households.)

Updating Mary’s picture with Lokol’s words


Bleeding starts → Family decides → Permission from elder → Motorbike arranged → Mother dies

The aha: “Family waits” was not really one box. It was two boxes — the deciding, and the permission. Mary did not see the permission box because she only sees what arrives at the clinic. Lokol saw it because he lived it.

Faith’s third interview — the county finance officer

Now Faith goes to the county headquarters and meets Esther, the finance officer.

She asks the opening question. Esther laughs gently.

esther

“I cannot tell you about deaths. I can tell you that we have run out of misoprostol — the drug that stops bleeding — three times this year, because the national supplier delivered late. We always pay on time. The drug just is not in the warehouse.”

A new noun appears far up the chain: stockout. It is nowhere near the bedside, but it is what made the bedside picture possible.

The picture grows again


National supplier delays → County stockout → Drug not at facility

⬇

Bleeding starts → Family decides → Permission → Motorbike → Mother arrives → Mother dies

Three people, three different parts of the picture. None of them was wrong. None of them had the whole thing.

Three traps when you do this

Trap 1 — Believing the loudest voice

The first person you interview is the most dangerous.

You go in, the midwife tells you a clear story, and you walk out thinking you have the picture. You stop interviewing.

Always interview at least one person from each of three groups: the bedside (midwives, families), the supply chain (finance, logistics), and the leadership (district medical officer, programme manager). Each group sees boxes the others cannot see.

Trap 2 — Drawing arrows you do not have evidence for

It is tempting to add arrows because they “feel right”.

The rule: every arrow on the picture should come from at least one specific sentence somebody said. If you cannot quote the source, the arrow is a hypothesis, not a fact — and you should mark it differently (we use a dotted arrow).

Trap 3 — Confusing “what people say” with “what is true”

People tell you their understanding of the system. Their understanding may be wrong.

That is fine. The point of the picture is not to be true on day one. It is to be specific enough that you can test it. The next chapters will teach you how to put numbers on this picture and see which arrows survive contact with data.

Try it yourself

You are the analyst

scenario

You have one week and a budget for petrol. You need to build a causal picture explaining why one ward in a Kenyan county has much higher under-5 mortality than its three neighbours.

Who do you interview, in what order, and what is the opening question for each?

Hint: who is closest to the death? Who is closest to the supply chain? Who is closest to the budget? Visit them in that order.

In Chapter 4, we will take a picture like Faith’s and start putting actual numbers on the arrows.

Looking ahead

In Chapter 4, you will take a finished interview-built picture and add the missing piece: numbers.

You will learn how to turn “Mary says about half the women bleed for more than thirty minutes before the family decides” into a number you can put on the arrow — and then how to combine all those numbers into a model that can be tested against real data.

Further reading

The data behind Faith’s story

  • Constitution of Kenya, 2010, Schedule 4 — the legal basis for devolution to 47 counties.
  • Kenya Health Information System (KHIS) — county dashboards with maternal mortality and stockout data, publicly available at hiskenya.org.
  • Bourbonnais N., 2013 — Implementing Free Maternal Health Care in Kenya: Challenges, Strategies, and Recommendations. Kenya National Commission on Human Rights. Open-access.

If you want to go deeper

  • Ryall, M. D. & Bramson, A. L. (2014) — Inference and Intervention. Routledge. Chapter 4 covers interview-driven model building in business settings; the method translates directly.
  • Schon, D. (1983) — The Reflective Practitioner. The classic on extracting models from people who “just know how the work works”.

The one thing to remember

The fastest way to build a useful causal picture is to ask the people who actually do the work — in three different groups, in a particular order — and draw their answers.

Faith built her picture in three interviews. None of them had the whole story. All of them needed each other.
